summary:
Moonbase Commander is a free browser game that helps children aged 7-12 explore space and learn how astronauts make decisions. Players join Pip, a friendly robot, on three Moon missions. They investigate possible water ice, manage a base’s battery and air supply, and explore a cave that could offer shelter.

The project addresses the challenge by turning space science and mission planning into activities children can try themselves. Players place scanners, compare clues, and send their findings to Earth. NASA images and research support the game’s science, while simulated readings and simple resource rules make it easier to understand.

We want to make space exploration feel exciting and accessible. By learning through play, children can build curiosity, practise problem-solving, and see why astronauts need evidence and careful planning.
details:
https://github.com/epicocookie/moonbase-cmder

Players interact with the game through walking, placing equipment, scanning samples, and making choices at the outpost’s stations. Pip gives a short instruction for the next task and offers hints when needed. Longer science explanations are available through “Learn more.”

We wanted the equipment to feel like part of the expedition. Scanners unfold their legs and collect readings with a visible scanning animation. A portable screen brings the findings together so players can compare them before sending a report. These actions connect the story with the science and give players a clear sense of progress.

The game is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Three.js handles the 3D world, lighting, models, and animations. Mission rules are kept separate from the visuals so the same calculations can support different views. The first two missions share progress between their 2D and 3D versions, while browser storage keeps active runs and completed reports.

We used Git and GitHub to combine our team’s work, GitHub Pages for hosting, and Node.js and Playwright to check mission rules and browser interactions. ChatGPT/Codex and Claude Code helped generate and revise substantial parts of the implementation. The credits page records AI assistance, NASA references, and third-party software.

Our main design considerations were readability, easy controls, scientific accuracy, and reliable gameplay. We shortened dialogue, added touch controls, and checked situations such as canceled scans, reloading a mission, and switching views. NASA imagery and research provide the references, while fictional readings and simplified resource rules are clearly identified.

We hope the game can support short learning activities at home or in classrooms, giving children a starting point for questions about how astronauts explore, gather evidence, and plan their missions.
